entities.summary: Constantine the Great (c. 272–337 CE) was the Roman Emperor whose conversion to Christianity and political patronage of the church permanently transformed Western civilisation. His Edict of Milan (313 CE) granted religious freedom throughout the empire, ending the Great Persecution. By defeating rivals Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge (312) and Licinius (324), he reunified the Roman Empire and became its sole ruler. He called and presided over the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE), which produced the Nicene Creed — still the central statement of Christian faith. In 330 CE he founded Constantinople (on the site of Byzantium), a new eastern capital that outlasted Rome by a millennium and became the heart of Byzantine civilisation. The Eastern Orthodox churches venerate him as a saint equal to the apostles.
